title.rendered: State police: Missing weapon in climate change battle?

content.rendered:
For years, Nigerians have debated the creation of state police almost exclusively through the prism of insecurity. The conversation has revolved around banditry, kidnapping, terrorism and violent crime. Yet, one crucial dimension has received scant attention: climate change.

Climate change is no longer merely an environmental issue. It has become a security challenge. Across Nigeria, forests are disappearing under the assault of illegal logging syndicates. Sand miners excavate riverbanks without restraint. Wetlands are reclaimed in defiance of environmental regulations. Grazing routes expand into protected ecosystems. Bush burning continues despite repeated warnings. Polluters dump hazardous wastes into rivers under the cover of darkness.

All these activities release greenhouse gases, destroy carbon sinks and worsen the country’s vulnerability to flooding, drought and desertification.

What is more, the recent statewide flooding in Lagos State has exposed another ecological reality that stares us in the face. People take advantage of rainfall to throw their domestic and industrial garbage into the waterways, culverts and manholes. These exacerbate the impact of the flooding on our environment. In fact, the ongoing Lagos-Calabar coastal highway is already being threatened by such callous and unpatriotic actions from citizens who should have known better.

The uncomfortable truth is that these environmental crimes flourish because enforcement is weak.

Nigeria operates a highly centralised policing structure. The Nigeria Police Force, despite the dedication of many officers, is overstretched. A force expected to combat terrorism, armed robbery, cybercrime, kidnapping, political violence and every imaginable criminal activity can hardly devote sufficient manpower to environmental offences.

Consequently, environmental laws are often treated as mere suggestions rather than binding regulations. Climate criminals understand this weakness.

Illegal loggers know that the chances of being arrested deep inside remote forests are slim. Unscrupulous miners know they can abandon excavated pits after extracting valuable minerals, leaving communities exposed to erosion and deadly accidents. Developers know they can build on floodplains because local authorities possess little enforcement capacity. The boys, girls, women and men who upend their dustbins into a flowing gutter assume that no authority figure is around the corner to call them to order.

The result is a silent assault on Nigeria’s ecological future. And this is where state police could become an unexpected climate solution.

Unlike a centrally controlled police force, state police would possess intimate knowledge of local geography, forests, rivers, wetlands and communities. Officers recruited from the local population would understand traditional land boundaries, seasonal environmental patterns and the identities of habitual offenders. Such familiarity makes environmental enforcement faster and more effective.

Imagine a state police command working closely with state ministries of environment, forestry departments, environmental health officers and local communities. Illegal chainsaw operators would be intercepted before entire forest reserves disappear. Sand mining along vulnerable riverbanks would attract immediate sanctions. Bush burning during the dry season could be prevented before wildfires spread across farmlands. And those everyday citizens waiting with their wastebaskets could be stopped before they toss their rubbish.

The impact would extend beyond environmental conservation. Nigeria loses enormous economic value through climate-induced disasters. Floods wash away roads, bridges, schools and hospitals. Desertification destroys agricultural land. Coastal erosion threatens communities across the Niger Delta. The cost of rebuilding after disasters is significantly higher than the cost of preventing environmental degradation in the first place. Climate adaptation, therefore, begins with law enforcement.

State police could also strengthen Nigeria’s commitment under international climate agreements. The country’s ambitious targets for reducing emissions and restoring degraded forests cannot be achieved through policy documents alone. Every climate policy requires boots on the ground. Someone must stop illegal logging. Someone must protect mangroves. Someone must arrest those poisoning rivers with industrial waste. Today, that “someone” is often absent.

Critics argue that state police could be abused by governors for political purposes. These concerns deserve serious consideration. However, the possibility of abuse should not become an excuse for institutional paralysis. Democratic societies build safeguards, not permanent excuses. Independent oversight commissions, judicial review, legislative scrutiny and constitutional limits can minimise political misuse while allowing states to address their peculiar security and environmental challenges.

Indeed, environmental protection itself is becoming a national security issue. Competition over shrinking natural resources already contributes to conflicts between farmers and herders. Desertification pushes populations southward. Flooding displaces thousands annually, creating humanitarian emergencies. Climate change multiplies existing social tensions. Preventing ecological destruction is therefore also preventing future conflicts. Environmental security and human security are inseparable.

Another often-overlooked benefit lies in emergency response. State police could become first responders during floods, erosion disasters, oil spills and wildfire outbreaks. Working alongside emergency management agencies, they could evacuate vulnerable communities, secure disaster zones and prevent looting during emergencies. Such rapid intervention would save lives while strengthening disaster resilience.

Furthermore, environmental law enforcement creates a culture of compliance. When citizens consistently see offenders prosecuted for illegal dumping, deforestation or encroachment into protected areas, respect for environmental regulations gradually becomes part of public consciousness. Laws influence behaviour only when they are enforced. This, I think, has been the major reason behind the seeming invisibility of the environmental health officers. They lack the bite to institute deterrence.

Nigeria’s climate policies will remain largely aspirational unless enforcement reaches the grassroots. The climate crisis is already knocking on our doors. We witness it in collapsing farmlands, drying rivers, disappearing forests, rising temperatures and devastating floods. Every year of delayed action increases both environmental damage and economic losses.

Perhaps, therefore, the debate on state police requires a broader perspective. It is not merely about who carries firearms. It is about who protects forests. Who safeguards wetlands? Who defends our rivers? Who preserves biodiversity? Who prevents environmental crimes before they become climate disasters? The future of Nigeria’s environmental security may depend as much on policing reform as on renewable energy, tree planting or international climate finance.

Environmental crimes are among the least prosecuted offences in many developing countries. Agencies responsible for environmental protection often struggle with inadequate funding, insufficient personnel, poor equipment, political interference and overlapping mandates. Where prosecutions occur, penalties are frequently too weak to deter repeat offenders. Climate policies cannot succeed where environmental crime pays.

The irony is striking. Developing countries gather annually at global climate conferences seeking climate finance, adaptation support and technology transfer. Yet much of the environmental destruction undermining climate resilience originates from illegal domestic activities that stronger governance could significantly reduce. Climate adaptation is impossible where lawlessness governs the environment.

Weak enforcement also discourages responsible investors. Companies willing to comply with environmental standards find themselves competing against operators who ignore regulations with little fear of sanctions. Over time, environmental compliance becomes a competitive disadvantage instead of a business norm. This governance deficit extends beyond environmental agencies; therefore, climate action requires an integrated security architecture.

A nation that cannot effectively protect its ecosystems cannot truly claim to be fighting climate change. And perhaps that is why the conversation on state police should no longer be confined to security experts alone. Environmentalists, climate scientists, public health professionals and policymakers all deserve a seat at the table. Because in the age of climate change, every environmental offence is also a security offence. And every effective police officer may become, in a very real sense, a climate defender.
